evidence: Callers now wait about 500 ms for currencyservice at p50, against 1.65 ms before the change (181 requests in the last 30 s). The service's own server spans are almost unchanged at 0.17 ms vs 0.14 ms, which points to roughly 500 ms of added network delay rather than slow processing. At t=26.5 s the pod started failing its liveness probe and is being killed and restarted. That event is still recurring, and the replica count now reads 0. Frontend is badly affected: p50 rose from 28 ms to 1034 ms, p95 is about 5 s, and errors are starting to appear (1.7%). Checkout had only 5 requests in the baseline and none since, so its impact is unmeasured but likely, because checkout calls currencyservice. Rolling back the change is the clear fix. Scaling up replicas or raising resource limits would not remove a network delay.

The change rolled out a new currencyservice pod at t≈2s. Its readiness probe failed twice with 'failed to connect within 1s', and the old pod was killed at t≈15s. In the last 10 s, callers' error rate for currencyservice rose from 0% to 82% (34 requests), and those failed calls returned almost instantly (p50 0.05 ms), while the service recorded no requests of its own. That pattern looks like refused connections (nothing accepting them), not slow processing. Over the 30 s window the caller error rate is 15.5% and rising. The failures are spreading: frontend errors are at 78% (36 requests) and all 4 checkout requests failed. Currencyservice memory dropped and CPU jumped to 53m, which fits a fresh or restarting container. There are no restart events yet, but past currencyservice incidents with similar early signs ended with the pod restarting repeatedly and 100% errors. Errors are already well above 5%, so High severity is likely; roll back the change. I can't tell for sure whether the root cause is a broken or unreachable pod or added network delay, so my confidence in the cause is moderate.

The change caused a normal rolling restart of paymentservice. A new pod (675788889c) was scheduled at +3s and started at +12s. Its liveness and readiness probes failed once or twice during startup (+14s to +16s), after which it became ready, and the old pod was removed at +25s. There is 1 replica and 0 restarts. Callers saw latency of 2.64 ms before vs 2.52 ms after, with 0% errors. That is only 4 vs 3 requests, too few to compare reliably, which is why confidence is low. No other service is significantly slower or returning errors. CPU (33m) and memory (87.7 MiB, up from 49) are higher on the new pod, which is normal when a process starts. The redeploy suggests a change to resource limits, but the telemetry doesn't show which limit. In similar past cases, CPU 125m and memory 160Mi limits ended Low, but a 128Mi memory limit ended High, with latency doubling by about 170s (still no restarts). Keep monitoring paymentservice memory, restarts and checkout latency for the next few minutes. If memory nears its limit or the pod restarts, roll the change back.

The change rolled out shippingservice as a new ReplicaSet. A new pod started about 6 s after the change and the old pod was then killed. Memory fell from 7.5 to about 3 MiB, as expected for a fresh pod. Replicas stayed at 1, there were no restarts and no probe-failure events. Even so, callers now see a 40% error rate over the last 30 s (45% over the last 15 s) against 0% before, and p95 latency of 12–13.6 s against 1.8 ms. That looks like requests timing out. Median latency rose from 0.98 to 2.5–3.8 ms. These numbers rest on only 20 requests, but both the slowdown and the extra errors are statistically significant. Frontend errors went from 0% to 12% and its p95 rose to 12 s, so the failures are reaching users. All other services look unchanged. Requests are still failing more than 20 s after the new pod started, so a normal rollout blip doesn't fully explain it. I can't pin down the cause: the median is too small to fit added network latency, and CPU and memory show no limit pressure. It is already High severity and getting no better, so roll back the change.

The change replaced the shippingservice pod: a new ReplicaSet scaled from 0 to 1 at t=4s, the old pod was stopped at t=6s, and there have been no restarts since. 1 replica is running. CPU is about 1m and steady. Memory fell from 6 to about 2.9 MiB, which is normal for a freshly started pod. Callers saw 54% errors over the last 30s and 43% over the last 15s, with p95 latency of 7-20s. That looks like calls stuck or dropped while the pods swapped, not slow processing: median latency in the last 15s is back to 1.16ms against a 1.01ms baseline. The sample is small, though (7 requests in the last 15s, 3 of them errors), so the error level has not yet been shown to be falling. The errors passed through to the frontend (12.5% errors, p95 spike). No other service is slower. The closest past incident, EXP_0308 (a CPU limit change on shippingservice that also replaced the pod), had 74% errors at 30s and recovered to Low by 170s. The past network-latency incidents showed restarts, Unhealthy events and 0 replicas, and none of that is happening here. I expect this to settle back to baseline. Keep watching the error rate over the next 1-2 minutes, and roll back if it is still above about 5%.

Every adservice call is failing now (40 of 40 in the last 30 s). Callers wait about 100 ms, then time out (p50 1.4 ms → 100.6 ms, about 70x slower). The readiness probe keeps failing because it cannot connect within 1 s. The pod is still up: 1 replica, no restarts, no new pod rolled out, and CPU (~2m) and memory (91.9 MiB) are unchanged. That rules out CPU, memory or unavailability as the cause and points to added network latency. The frontend is the only other service hit: p50 went from 18 ms to 116 ms, with no errors because it carries on without ads. Two past adservice incidents with 100 ms and 300 ms of added network latency looked the same, with errors near 100% and a slower frontend, and both stayed High at 170 s.

Callers now wait about 103 ms for emailservice, up from a 2.8 ms baseline (p50, about 37x slower, p=0.0027). emailservice's own server spans are unchanged (0.29 to 0.35 ms, not significant), so the extra time is being added on the network, not inside the service. CPU (about 4 millicores) and memory (36.5 MiB) are flat, there have been no restarts, the single replica is still running, there are no events and there are no errors. Nothing in the telemetry shows the change doing anything to paymentservice yet, but the evidence is thin. The pod did not restart or roll out: no Kubernetes events, still 1 replica, 0 restarts. Past paymentservice limit changes all showed a pod rollout and a big CPU jump by 30 s. Here CPU (~1m) and memory (~49.5 MiB) are flat. Keep watching paymentservice latency and errors as checkouts come in.

Callers now wait about 1 s for currencyservice: p50 went from 2.2 ms to 1002 ms, roughly 450x its baseline, with p95 at 1005 ms. The change started a rollout. A new recommendationservice pod was scheduled at 3 s. Its readiness probe began failing at 5 s and its liveness probe at 9 s, with 'failed to connect within 1s' timeouts, and the kubelet killed it for failing liveness at 19 s. These probe-failure and kill events are still repeating, so the pod is crash-looping. Requests are still being served normally (probably by the old pod, though that is not confirmed): p50 is 4.0 ms against a 4.2 ms baseline, errors are 0%, and the replica count is still 1. CPU jumped to 39m and memory rose from 32 to 50 MiB at 30 s, which looks like the new pod repeatedly starting up. Of the past recommendationservice incidents returned, the closest match is EXP_0297 (CPU limit set to 100m): a new pod failing its probes, 4 restarts by 170 s, latency unchanged, and a final severity of High. The other similar incidents were network-latency changes, and those showed huge latency, errors and 0 replicas at 30 s, which is not what we see here. Nobody can see the change content, so 'cpu_limit' is inferred and not confirmed. Repeated restarts count as High severity. Callers are not affected yet, but the rollout will not complete while the new pod keeps failing, so rolling back is the safest action.

The change started a rollout. A new pod (5678f8bb94) was created at t+3s and failed its readiness probe at t+6s (it could not connect within 1s). The old pod was killed at the same moment anyway. Callers of productcatalogservice now see errors: 12.8% over the last 30s, rising to 28% over the last 10s, against 0% in the 754-request baseline. Caller p95 latency jumped from 2 ms to about 16 s, meaning some calls hang until they time out. The service's own server spans show no errors and unchanged latency (p50 0.1 ms), so the failures happen at connection or availability level, not in the service's processing. The pod has 1 replica and no restarts, and its CPU and memory are low after the restart, so there is no evidence of a resource limit being hit. Knock-on effects: frontend errors are at 35% with p95 about 20 s, and recommendationservice's callers see 11% errors with p95 about 14 s. The error rate is far above the 5% High threshold and still climbing. The exact mechanism is unclear, so confidence is moderate.

The change triggered a normal rolling update. A new pod was scheduled, pulled, created and started within about 5 s, and the old pod was stopped. Past checkoutservice resource-limit changes that showed this same rollout event pattern ended at Low severity. The change started a rolling update of cartservice: a new ReplicaSet 59f6575bfc and a new pod were created at about t+3.5s. The change triggered a rolling update. The new currencyservice pod started at about +5s. I picked Medium, which fits a throttled service whose latency is rising. If the latency or probe failures get worse, raise the CPU limit or roll back the change.

The change caused a normal rolling update. Events show a new productcatalogservice pod (v0.10.5) was scheduled and started at about 5 s, and the old pod was killed at about 6 s. The change rolled out a new recommendationservice pod (scheduled at about 3 s). Its readiness probe failed 3 times and its liveness probe failed 2 times while it was starting. Thirty seconds after the change, checkoutservice requests take about 3.0 s at the median as callers see them, up from about 46 ms, and 2.8 s in its own server spans. That is more than 60 times its baseline. The sample is small (2 baseline and 4 recent requests), so the comparison is not statistically reliable. Every call checkoutservice makes to the services it depends on now takes about 200 ms longer from checkoutservice's side: email 2.6 ms to 203 ms, payment 2.8 ms to 204 ms, and the currency p95 2 ms to 4 ms rose to about 202 ms. Those services' own processing times have not changed (email 0.23 ms, payment 0.28 ms). Callers also see about 200 ms more than checkoutservice's own spans show. Together this points to delay added on checkoutservice's network path, not slow processing. CPU stays around 1 millicore and memory at 8.1 MiB, with 1 replica, no restarts, no Kubernetes events and no errors, so a resource limit or crash is unlikely. Other services' medians are unchanged. Frontend's p95 rose from 78 ms to 114 ms, which fits checkout requests being slow. Because latency is far more than double the baseline, I expect High severity and recommend rolling back the change.

Frontend's median latency jumped from 15 ms to about 1116 ms (p95 30 ms to 1426 ms, p=2e-22). That is far more than double the baseline, so this is High severity. Error rate is still 0. Every outbound call the frontend makes now takes about 100 ms longer as measured by the caller: currency 1.4 to 102 ms, productcatalog 0.6 to 101 ms, recommendation 3.8 to 104 ms, checkout 18 to 119 ms. The downstream services' own processing times are basically unchanged. That pattern means added network delay on the frontend's side, not slow downstream services. Checkout is listed as affected because users waiting on it see the extra delay; its own processing is not slower, and that comparison rests on only 4 recent requests. No other services are slower. This is based on only 30 s of data, but the effect is large and consistent. Recommend rolling back the change.

Confidence is only moderate. The last 10s contain very few traces (3 calls to productcatalogservice, 2 of them errors; 2 frontend requests at a median of 779 ms), possibly because traces are exported with a delay. I can't rule out an ongoing problem or tell which resource setting was changed. Keep watching: if errors or latency continue past the rollout, roll the change back.

The change was a normal rolling update. A new paymentservice pod started at about 3 s. Its readiness probe failed twice in the first few seconds, which is usual while a pod starts up. After that it served traffic, and the old pod was removed at 15 s. There is still 1 replica with 0 restarts. Memory is steady at about 39-42 MiB. CPU rose to 31m at 30 s, which is consistent with the new pod warming up. Callers see a median latency of 2.46 ms now against 2.8 ms before (not slower) and no errors. No other service is measurably slower or returning errors. Confidence is limited for two reasons. First, there is very little payment traffic: 3 caller requests in the last 30 s and 8 in the baseline. Second, a past incident that looked the same at 30 s (a 128Mi memory limit on this service) got worse later, with latency roughly doubling. So keep watching latency and restarts for the next few minutes.

Callers now wait much longer for currencyservice: p50 went from 1.35 ms to 51.5 ms and p95 from 2.44 ms to 52.4 ms, a jump of about 38x (p=2.7e-103, 222 requests). Its own server spans barely changed (0.14 ms to 0.19 ms), so roughly 50 ms of fixed delay is being added on the network path, not in processing. CPU (~11m), memory (~50 MiB), replicas (1) and restarts (0) are all flat, and there are no Kubernetes events. Errors are 0%. Frontend has slowed as a knock-on effect: p50 went from 17 ms to 116 ms and p95 from 33 ms to 523 ms. Checkoutservice also looks slower (16 ms to 168 ms), but that is based on only 3 requests. Other services are unchanged. Latency is far more than double the baseline, so severity is High; rolling back the change is the recommended action.

Frontend's own server spans went from p50 16 ms to 294 ms (+1744%) and p95 from 38 ms to 409 ms, based on 68 requests (p=1e-26). Errors stayed at 0. Every call frontend makes now takes about 25 ms longer from frontend's side: productcatalog 0.8 to 26 ms, currency 1.4 to 27 ms, recommendation 4 to 29 ms. The downstream services' own server spans barely changed, about 0.1-2.5 ms. That pattern points to delay added to frontend's network traffic, not slow downstream processing. Frontend CPU (about 15-19m) and memory (about 15 MiB) are flat, there are no restarts or pod events, and replicas stay at 1, so it is not a CPU or memory limit. Frontend latency is already more than double its baseline, which meets High. Only frontend (and the users behind it) is degraded; the other services look worse only from frontend's side.

The change rolled out a new pod (ReplicaSet 8545db795f). Its readiness probe started failing at 6s and its liveness probe at 10s, with 'failed to connect within 1s' timeouts. At 20s Kubernetes killed it for failing liveness, and the restart count went from 19 to 20. The old pod was then deleted at 25s, so only the failing pod is left. Probe timeouts while the pod starts up, with memory only rising a little (33→38 MiB, no OOM), point to a CPU limit starving the process. This matches past incident EXP_0297, where a 100m CPU limit on recommendationservice gave the same rollout and probe-failure pattern with latency unchanged at 30s, and it ended High with repeated restarts. Callers' latency is unchanged for now (p50 4.3→4.5ms, 0 errors), probably because requests were still served by the old pod until it was deleted. No other service is degraded yet. I expect a crash loop (High), so roll back the change. Confidence is moderate because the cause is inferred from the pattern; the content of the change is unknown.

The change was a normal rolling replacement. A new checkoutservice pod started, failed one readiness probe at startup and then took over from the old pod. Replicas stayed at 1 with 0 restarts. CPU (about 5m) and memory (about 5Mi) are low and still rising, which is what a freshly started pod looks like. checkoutservice served only 1 request in the last 30 s, taking about 2.9 s against a 22 ms baseline, and its own server span shows the same delay. That fits a cold start (new connections being set up) on the first request, but one request is too few to tell for sure. No other service is measurably slower or returning errors: frontend, payment, email, shipping and currency are all at baseline. In five similar past checkoutservice rollouts (CPU or memory limit changes), there were brief early spikes, including one with a 46,000% latency jump and 75% errors at 30 s, and all of them settled to Low severity by 170 s. Watch checkoutservice latency and restarts over the next few minutes, and roll back if requests stay over 2x the baseline or the pod starts restarting.

The change triggered a rolling update. A new currencyservice pod was started, and its liveness probe failed at about 15 s because it could not connect within 1 s, which suggests the pod is starved of CPU. The old pod was then stopped. Replicas stay at 1 and there are no restarts yet. CPU jumped to 79m, against a baseline of about 30m, while memory dropped to 38 MiB because the pod is new. In the last 10 s the service is clearly slower and the test is significant (p≈1e-26): callers' p50 went from 1.87 to 2.77 ms (+48%) and p95 from 4 to 68 ms. The service's own server spans are also slower (p50 +37%), so the slowdown is in processing, not the network. Traffic is high. Frontend errors rose to 1.1% and currencyservice errors to 0.3%. Past incidents with the same pattern (new pod, failed probe, CPU spike) were mostly CPU limits of 100–125m, which ended High severity. Memory-limit changes look similar early on and ended Low, so the cause is not certain. Confidence is moderate because the latency data covers only 10 s.

The change rolled out a new currencyservice pod (new ReplicaSet created at t+3s, old pod killed at t+27s). The new pod failed its readiness probe 4 times and its liveness probe twice in its first ~20s, timing out after 1s each time. That points to a slow, resource-starved start. One more liveness failure would probably restart it. CPU rose from about 30m to 77m and memory from 48 to 88.5 MiB as the new pod took traffic. A CPU limit seems more likely than a memory limit because the probes timed out connecting rather than the pod running out of memory, but this lean is not strong. So far callers see no difference: latency is unchanged (p50 1.7ms vs 1.69ms, p95 4.34ms vs 3.84ms in the last 10s, not significant), errors are 0, no restarts yet, and no other service is affected. This rollout pattern closely matches two past incidents where currencyservice's CPU limit was set to 100m; both ended as High severity even though latency at 30s looked normal. It also resembles a past 192Mi memory-limit change that ended Low, so the cause is uncertain. The new pod has only had about 3s of traffic, so the evidence is weak and my confidence is low. I recommend rolling back the change.

The change rolled out a new paymentservice pod. The new ReplicaSet came up at t≈4 s and failed readiness and liveness probes 4 times while starting (t≈6–17 s). It then became ready, and the old pod was removed at t≈26 s. There is 1 replica and 0 restarts. Latency is unchanged: callers see p50 2.6 ms before vs 2.1 ms now, and the service's own spans show 0.43 ms vs 0.31 ms. There are no errors. Checkoutservice is not measurably slower (p=0.46). The weak point is the sample size: only 3 requests in the last 30 s, so the latency numbers say little. At t=30 s, CPU jumped to 40 m and memory to 82 MiB (from 45 MiB). This could be normal startup, which is common for this service. Past incidents with the same rollout pattern were mostly resource-limit changes (memory 128–160Mi, CPU 150m) and mostly ended Low. A few ended Medium or High (CPU 150m, memory 128Mi), so keep watching memory in case it climbs towards an OOM kill, and watch CPU throttling and latency over the next few minutes.

Callers now wait about 500 ms at p50 for cartservice, up from 1.4 ms (p95 rose from 2.7 to 752 ms), across 68 requests (p=3e-32). That is far more than double its baseline, which counts as High. Error rate is still 0%. CPU stayed flat at about 7m and memory at about 67.6 MiB, with no new restarts or pod events, so this is not CPU throttling, memory pressure or the service being down. A steady delay of about 500 ms with nothing changing in resources points to added network latency. cartservice exports no spans of its own, so I couldn't confirm the network cause by comparing its own timings with what callers see. The delay is reaching its callers: frontend p50 went from 20.5 to 521 ms (significant), and checkoutservice went from about 18 to 1021 ms, but that is based on only 2 requests. Other services are unchanged. Rolling back the change is recommended.

Seen by its callers, emailservice p50 went from 2.9 ms to about 253 ms, an ~87x increase and well over double its baseline. Its own server spans are unchanged (about 0.3 ms), so the added time is in the network, not in processing. There are no errors. CPU and memory are flat, and there are no restarts or Kubernetes events. checkoutservice is significantly slower (p50 17 ms to 269 ms, p=0.006), and that delay goes up to frontend's checkout calls, though I didn't check frontend directly. Confidence is lowered because the sample is tiny: only 3 requests in the last 30 s against 8 in the baseline, so the emailservice test alone isn't significant (p=0.04). Still, the delay is very consistent at about 250 ms.

Measured 30 s after the change. recommendationservice's own server spans went from a median of 2.5 ms to about 603 ms, a near-constant extra ~600 ms. CPU stayed flat at ~12 millicores and memory didn't change before the restart, so it isn't running out of CPU or memory. Its calls to productcatalogservice also take ~600 ms at p95 as seen by the caller, while productcatalogservice's own spans are still ~0.1 ms. That points to delay added on recommendationservice's network path, not slow code. Its liveness probe started failing at t+13 s and is still failing. The container was killed and restarted, and replicas are now 0. Callers see 41.5% errors and p95 of 1208 ms against a 7.5 ms baseline, so this is High. The impact spreads to frontend: p95 rose from 42 ms to 1226 ms and p50 is up 21%, which is statistically significant. Other services are unchanged. The cause is less certain than the severity: the restart could also mean the service is simply down, but the pattern of extra delay fits network latency best. Recommend rolling back the change.

Callers of adservice now see a median latency of 100.6 ms (p95 101.1 ms), up from a 3.8 ms baseline, and 97% of calls fail. Nearly every call ending at about 100 ms points to a client-side timeout. The adservice pod itself looks normal: 1 replica, no restarts, no Kubernetes events, and CPU and memory unchanged. A slow network to the pod fits that picture better than the pod being down. Frontend median latency went from 20 ms to 116 ms (+480%). No other service is measurably slower. In past incidents where 400-450 ms of network latency was added to adservice, the early signs matched this one (very high latency and 95-100% errors at 30 s). Both ended High, with probe failures, restarts and 0 replicas by about 170 s. Severity is already above the High threshold, so I recommend rolling back now. This is only 30 s after the change, and the cause is inferred from the latency pattern and past incidents, not seen directly.

The change rolled out a new adservice ReplicaSet. A new pod was scheduled and started at about +5 s, with no restarts and no Unhealthy events so far, and replicas stayed at 1. At +30 s, CPU rose from about 25m to 105m and memory from about 85 to 139 MiB. That looks like the new JVM pod starting up while the old pod is still running, but there are only a few samples, so it is not certain. As callers see it, adservice is unchanged: 63 requests in the last 30 s, p50 2.94 ms against 3.07 ms baseline, p95 5.57 against 6.57 ms, and 0% errors. No other service is significantly slower or failing. Past adservice incidents with this same pattern (new pod rolled out, CPU and memory spike at 30 s, latency flat) were CPU or memory limit changes. Most ended Low, but one (CPU limit 200m) ended Medium. I can't yet tell whether this is a CPU or a memory limit, or confirm that the rollout will finish cleanly, so the operator should keep watching for throttling, out-of-memory kills or a latency rise over the next few minutes.

At t=0 the currencyservice deployment was scaled down from 1 replica to 0. Its pod was killed and metrics show 0 replicas at t=15 s and t=30 s. As seen by its callers, currencyservice errors went from 0% to 23.5% and p95 latency from 4.7 ms to about 16.9 s (timeouts). The requests that still succeeded were fast, with own server spans unchanged, so the problem is that nothing is serving, not slow processing. Frontend errors rose from 0% to 44% with p95 around 18.5 s. Checkoutservice failed on 2 of only 3 requests, which is too few to measure well, but it calls currencyservice, so it will keep failing while currencyservice is down. Other services are normal. Nothing scales the deployment back up, so it will stay unavailable until the change is rolled back.

The change scaled the emailservice deployment from 1 replica to 0. Kubernetes logged ScalingReplicaSet and Killing events at t=0, metrics show 0 replicas at t=+15s, and the pod failed its readiness probe because it could not connect. Callers of emailservice now get 100% errors, with p50 16.8s against 2.4ms at baseline. emailservice logged no server spans in the last 30s, so nothing is serving it. checkoutservice waits on emailservice, and its p50 rose from 20ms to 16.8s (p<0.001), though it still reports no errors. Frontend latency overall is unchanged because checkout is a small share of its traffic. The sample is small (5 requests in the last 30s), but having 0 replicas means emailservice is unavailable, so severity is High. Roll back the change to restore the replica.

The change was a normal rolling update. A new pod (b8c4f67b5) started at t+4s and the old pod was removed at t+6s. The new pod failed one readiness probe at startup, which is usual while a container is coming up. Since then it has had no restarts and still has 1 replica. Latency as callers see it: p50 is 0.92 ms against a 0.89 ms baseline (+3%, p=0.44) with 0 errors. In the last 15 s, p95 is back to 1.85 ms (baseline 1.82). The brief p95 spike to 8 ms in the 30 s window happened during the pod swap. CPU (about 2 millicores) and memory (3.5 MiB, reset by the restart) are low and not climbing toward a limit. No other service is significantly slower or returning errors. Past shippingservice incidents with real impact showed repeated restarts and latency hundreds of times higher by 30 s, and none of that is happening here. The main caveat is that shippingservice served only about 25 requests in the window, and a resource-limit change could still show up later. Keep monitoring for a few minutes.

The events show a normal rolling update: a new frontend pod started at about +5 s and the old pod was deleted at +15 s. No restarts or probe failures so far, and the replica count stayed at 1. That pattern matches past incidents where a resource limit was changed. The new pod is getting slower. Over the last 30 s, p50 latency rose from 16.4 to 20.7 ms (+26%) and p95 from 44 to 103 ms. Over the last 15 s, p50 is 38.7 ms (+136%) and p95 is 474 ms. The last 15 s contains only 12 requests, so that figure is uncertain. Throughput fell sharply: about 1.6 req/s in the last 30 s and 0.8 req/s in the last 15 s, against about 6.6 req/s at baseline. That looks like the frontend can't keep up. Downstream services are not the cause: currency, productcatalog and recommendation show the same latency in their own spans, and no other service is significantly slower. There are no errors. The new pod's CPU sits near 35-42m without rising while latency climbs, which suggests a low CPU limit is throttling it. That is an inference: the change itself is unknown and there is no throttling metric. Memory on the new pod is 4.4 MiB, which is a fresh process, though a very tight memory limit can't be ruled out. Past CPU-limit changes to frontend ended at Medium, but here latency is already more than double baseline and getting worse, so I predict High. Recommend rolling back the change.

About 15 s after the change, emailservice started failing its liveness probe and Kubernetes killed the pod. The Killing event is still recurring. At t=30 s the service has 0 replicas and 1 restart, and memory has dropped from 36.5 to 2.7 MiB (-93%). Severity looks High because the service is down and restarting. Traffic is too low to compare latency or error rates: 2 requests in the baseline and none since the change, for both emailservice and checkoutservice. The cause is a less certain inference. There are no ScalingReplicaSet or new-pod events, only probe-triggered kills, and that matches two past emailservice incidents with added network latency (EXP_0369, EXP_0338). Both had 0 replicas and -93% memory at 30 s, then went into a restart loop with 100% errors. Past CPU and memory-limit incidents showed ScalingReplicaSet events, which we don't see here. Nothing shows other services degraded yet, but confirmation emails from checkout will fail while emailservice is down. Roll back the change.
